newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan rupee set to hit new lows -- analysts.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan rupee set to hit new lows -- analysts.

text.p: The Sri Lankan rupee, hovering around an all-time low against the dollar, is set to plumb new depths in the months ahead, analysts and foreign exchange dealers said on Tuesday.
They said the rupee, which fell to a record low of 56.40 to the U.S. unit on Monday, could fall a further five percent in the next three or four months.
"We will, of course, see more lows in months to come," said Wasantha Alutwela, a dealer at Standard Chartered Bank in Colombo.
"The rupee is rising (on Tuesday) mainly because of the central bank's action," Alutwela said, adding it had allowed the local unit to fall by about five percent since the beginning of this year.

The rupee clawed back to 56.12 to the dollar by midday on Tuesday, but a survey of five economists and dealers showed they expected the rate to dip to between 57.5 and 59.5 by the end of the year, against 53.62 at the beginning of 1996.

Econsult, a private economic consultancy firm, said in a recent report that many private sector economists had called for a devaluation of the rupee to stop exports slumping and provide a momentum for a recovery.

The report said under normal circumstances "a devaluation in the order of some 20 percent would do the trick". But it cautioned against such a move, citing the intensified war between government troops and Tamil Tiger rebels that badly hit the economy and damaged the industrial base.
"In itself, a major devaluation would do little to boost exports and may even do more harm than good to the economy as a whole," it said.
Economists said such a move would worsen already high inflation as Colombo tried to import expensive war equipment and food to meet shortages caused by drought earlier this year.
With eight-month defence spending overshooting the 1996 budget by one-third, annualised inflation soared to 13.9 percent in August, the highest since October 1991 when it was 14.2 percent.
Azra Jafferjee, an economist at Jardine Fleming, said the central bank had traditionally let the rupee slide gradually against the dollar and was expected to continue this policy for the time being.

"Domestic inflation right now takes priority," she said."If you have a sharp devaluation that would increase the domestic financing cost even more. All these things combined will make sure the government will not go for a devaluation this year."
Jafferjee said she expected consumer price inflation to rise to 14.7 percent this year against a 7.7 percent gain last year.

She put the rupee-dollar exchange rate at 59.5 for end-1996, saying the Central Bank would have to let the local currency fall in view of the inflation differential between Sri Lanka and the United States.

Economists said foreign exchange reserves had fallen in the past few months to a level enough to cover 4-1/2 months of imports, against five months at the end of last year, fuelling speculation on the foreign exchange market that the central bank would have to let the rupee fall faster against the dollar.

"But the government cannot afford to let it (the rupee) fall too much in view of the continuing ethnic war that requires imports of arms as well as daily necessities," said research head Nanda Nair of SBS Keelles brokerage.
Nair said Sri Lanka's reserve position was still well above the critical level of the equivalent of three months of imports.
